citations.quote: **(a) Lorentzian metric.** The field $g$ is a **Lorentzian metric of signature $(-,+,+,+)$** on $M$ when it is symmetric and nondegenerate, and at every $p\in M$ the pair $(T_pM,g_p)$ is a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ in the sense of [[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]: that is, $g_p$ has inertia $(3,1,0)$, so that some — equivalently every — basis of $T_pM$ in which the matrix of $g_p$ is diagonal has exactly one negative and three positive diagonal entries.
An orientation of an $n$-manifold is a smooth choice of a ray in $\det T_pM$ for every $p$.

**(a) Observers.** An **observer at $p$** is a tangent vector $n\in T_pM$ such that $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $n$ is future-directed in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]], that is, $g_p(n,N_p)<0$.
$\dim n^{\perp}=3$ and the restriction of $g_p$ to $n^{\perp}$ is positive definite.

**(a) Congruences.** An **observer congruence** on $U$ is a smooth vector field $n$ on $U$ ([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]) such that $n_q$ is an observer at $q$ for every $q\in U$ ([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]); explicitly, $$g_q(n_q,n_q)=-1\quad\text{and}\quad g_q(n_q,N_q)<0\qquad\text{for every }q\in U .$$ Since $g_q(n_q,n_q)=-1$, the field $n$ is nowhere vanishing.

**(c) Tetrad fields.** A **tetrad field** (or **$g$-orthonormal frame field**) on $U$ is a local frame field $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ on $U$ such that $$g_q(E_A(q),E_B(q))=\eta_{AB}\qquad\text{for all }A,B\text{ and all }q\in U .$$ A tetrad field is **future-directed** when in addition $E_0(q)$ is future-directed for every $q\in U$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]); then each $E_0(q)$ is an observer at $q$ ([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]), so $E_0$ is an observer congruence on $U$ ([[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]), while $E_1,E_2,E_3$ are pointwise an orthonormal basis of the rest space of that observer.
**(c) Metric-selected connections.** A **metric-selected connection** for $(M,g)$ is an affine connection on $M$ that is both torsion-free and $g$-compatible.

**(b) Coordinate formula.** In every smooth chart $(U,x)$ with Christoffel symbols $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ of $\nabla$ ([[def-christoffel-symbols-of-an-affine-connection]]), $$R^a{}_{bcd}=\partial_c\Gamma^a{}_{db}-\partial_d\Gamma^a{}_{cb} +\sum_e\bigl(\Gamma^a{}_{ce}\Gamma^e{}_{db}-\Gamma^a{}_{de}\Gamma^e{}_{cb}\bigr)$$ on $U$, for all $a,b,c,d\in\{0,1,2,3\}$.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and $$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$ For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with $$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following statement.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$. Finite componentwise sums and products of $C^k$ Euclidean maps are $C^k$, and a composite of composable $C^k$ Euclidean maps is $C^k$. Scalar multiples are included among the finite componentwise operations. The assertions remain valid on an empty open domain.

derivations.claim: The normalization $n:=N/\sqrt{-g(N,N)}$ is smooth because $-g(N,N)$ is a smooth positive function and [F5] makes its positive square root smooth. Bilinearity gives $g(n,n)=-1$ and $g(n,N)=-\sqrt{-g(N,N)}<0$, so [F2] makes $n$ an observer at every point and hence a smooth observer congruence. This supplies an observer field without identifying it with a chart or tetrad.

Fix $p\in U$ and a connected chart around $p$. The four coordinate vectors form a basis at $p$. By [F2], the linear map $h_{n_p}$ has image the three-dimensional space $n_p^\perp$, so three projected coordinate vectors form a basis of $n_p^\perp$. Extend the chosen coordinate fields over the chart and project them by $h_n$; after shrinking the chart, their projections remain independent by continuity. They lie in the positive-definite rest spaces by [F2]. Apply the three finite Gram-Schmidt operations in these rest spaces; every denominator is the positive square root of a positive smooth squared norm, so [F5] makes the resulting fields smooth. Together with $E_0=n$, the three fields form a local tetrad. If needed, reverse one spatial member so the tetrad has the supplied orientation from [F1]; the sign remains fixed on the connected chart. This is a local tetrad field as in [F3], not a coordinate frame or an assertion of an adapted coordinate chart. Thus an $n$-adapted tetrad exists locally, with no global tetrad or hypersurface-orthogonality conclusion.

In a length-coordinate chart, each first coordinate derivative of $g_{ab}$ has dimension $\mathrm m^{-1}$, so the Christoffel formula in [F4] has dimension $\mathrm m^{-1}$. Each term in the curvature formula in [F4] has dimension $\mathrm m^{-2}$; contraction with dimensionless $g^{ab}$ preserves that dimension for Ricci and scalar curvature. This is coordinate-unit bookkeeping, not a physical field equation.

citations.quote: For every observer congruence $n$, each point has a neighborhood carrying an $n$-adapted tetrad; this is a local assertion only.

**(c) Tetrad fields.** A **tetrad field** (or **$g$-orthonormal frame field**) on $U$ is a local frame field $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ on $U$ such that $$g_q(E_A(q),E_B(q))=\eta_{AB}\qquad\text{for all }A,B\text{ and all }q\in U .$$ A tetrad field is **future-directed** when in addition $E_0(q)$ is future-directed for every $q\in U$ ([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]); then each $E_0(q)$ is an observer at $q$ ([[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]), so $E_0$ is an observer congruence on $U$ ([[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]), while $E_1,E_2,E_3$ are pointwise an orthonormal basis of the rest space of that observer.

That these local forms agree on chart overlaps and therefore define one smooth nowhere-vanishing $4$-form $\mathrm{vol}_g$ on $M$ — the **metric volume form** — is proved in [[lem-gr-metric-volume-form-patching-and-face-normal]] clause (a), together with the reading statement of clause (b) there: in every oriented chart $\mathrm{vol}_g=w\,dx^0\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^3$, and on every positively oriented $g_p$-orthonormal basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $T_pM$ one has $\mathrm{vol}_{g,p}(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=1$.

Then $$\det(g'_{ab})=\bigl(\det D\varphi\bigr)^{2}\det\bigl(g_{ab}\circ\varphi\bigr),\qquad w'=\bigl(\det D\varphi\bigr)\,(w\circ\varphi),$$ and the local forms agree on the overlap, $$\varphi^{*}\bigl(w\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3\bigr)=w'\,dy^0\wedge dy^1\wedge dy^2\wedge dy^3 .$$ Consequently there is a unique smooth nowhere-vanishing $4$-form $\mathrm{vol}_g$ on $M$ — the **metric volume form** — whose restriction to the domain of every oriented chart $(U,x)$ is $w\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$; it is a smooth section with nowhere-zero values and positive on the given orientation.
A **smooth differential $k$-form** on $M$ is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M\to M$.

On a chart $(U,x^1,\ldots,x^n)$, every smooth differential $k$-form $\omega$ has a unique expression $$ \omega=\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n}\omega_{i_1\cdots i_k}\,dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k} $$ with smooth coefficient functions $\omega_{i_1\cdots i_k}$ on $U$.
Their **wedge product** is the differential form defined pointwise by $$ (\alpha\wedge\beta)_p:=\alpha_p\wedge\beta_p\in\operatorname{Alt}^{k+\ell}(T_pM).
The graded vector space $$ \Omega^*(M):=\bigoplus_{k\ge 0}\Omega^k(M) $$ with the wedge product is an associative graded-commutative algebra.

For $\omega\in\Omega^k(M)$, define the candidate $d\omega$ on smooth vector fields by $$d\omega(X_0,\ldots,X_k)=\sum_i(-1)^iX_i\omega(X_0,\widehat X_i,\ldots,X_k)+\sum_{i<j}(-1)^{i+j}\omega([X_i,X_j],X_0,\widehat X_i,\widehat X_j,\ldots,X_k).$$ The next lemma proves that this candidate is a form.
The invariant formula defining $d\omega$ is alternating and $C^\infty(M)$-multilinear in $X_0,\ldots,X_k$; hence it defines a smooth $(k+1)$-form.
Summing over increasing $k$-tuples $I$, and writing $dx^I=dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k}$, if $\omega=\sum_I\omega_I\,dx^I$, then $$d\omega=\sum_I d\omega_I\wedge dx^I.$$
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.
For homogeneous smooth forms $\alpha\in\Omega^p(M)$ and $\beta\in\Omega^q(M)$, $$d(\alpha\wedge\beta)=d\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^{\deg\alpha}\alpha\wedge d\beta.$$

**Inverse metric.** The **inverse metric** at $p$ is the symmetric bilinear form $$g_p^{-1}:T_p^*M\times T_p^*M\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta).$$ It is symmetric because $g_p$ is, and it is nondegenerate: if $g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta)=0$ for all $\beta$, then $g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\cdot)=0$, so $\sharp_p\alpha=0$ and hence $\alpha=0$.

derivations.claim: The determinant is alternating multilinear in each list, so it defines a bilinear pairing on exterior powers. In a positively oriented orthonormal coframe, it makes the basis wedges $e^I$ orthogonal with squared norm $\epsilon_I$; in the full component contraction this same diagonal value occurs $k!$ times, canceled by the factor $1/k!$. Define $\star_g e^I=\epsilon_I s(I,I^c)e^{I^c}$ and extend linearly. If $J\ne I$ has the same size as $I$, then $e^J\wedge e^{I^c}=0$ because an index repeats. If $J=I$, then $e^I\wedge e^{I^c}=s(I,I^c)\mathrm{vol}_g$, so $e^I\wedge\star_g e^I=\epsilon_I\mathrm{vol}_g$. Bilinearity proves the characterizing identity for all forms in the coframe. The complement wedges pair each basis vector with exactly one basis vector, so this wedge pairing is nondegenerate and the characterization determines $\star_g$ uniquely.

The characterizing identity uses only $g$, the orientation, and $\mathrm{vol}_g$. Any other positively oriented orthonormal coframe therefore defines the same map by uniqueness. In each smooth tetrad neighborhood the displayed matrix of $\star_g$ is constant in the smooth coframe, so its coordinate coefficients are smooth; the locally defined maps agree on overlaps and give a global smooth bundle map.

Applying the basis formula twice gives $\star_g^2e^I=\epsilon_I\epsilon_{I^c}s(I,I^c)s(I^c,I)e^I$. The product $\epsilon_I\epsilon_{I^c}$ equals $-1$ because exactly one of the four $\epsilon_i$ is negative. Reversing the two blocks of sizes $k$ and $4-k$ takes $k(4-k)$ transpositions, so $s(I,I^c)s(I^c,I)=(-1)^{k(4-k)}$. Their product is $(-1)^{k(4-k)+1}$, proving the square formula for each basis element and hence for every $k$-form.

For a two-form $F=\frac12F_{cd}e^c\wedge e^d$, the basis formula sends each $e^c\wedge e^d$ to its oriented complementary wedge with the product of its metric signs. In components this is $({\star_gF})_{ab}=\frac12(\mathrm{vol}_g)_{abcd}F^{cd}$: the factor $1/2$ counts each antisymmetric pair once, and raising both indices includes the negative sign in the timelike slot.

In a chart, [F4] gives $(d\alpha)_{a_0\cdots a_k}=(k+1)\partial_{[a_0}\alpha_{a_1\cdots a_k]}$. Applying it twice expresses each coefficient of $d^2\alpha$ as an alternating sum of second partial derivatives; terms paired by exchanging the first two derivative indices cancel because those mixed partials agree by [F5]. Thus $d^2\alpha=0$ in every chart and hence globally. The graded product rule is exactly the established identity in [F5].

Fix a point and use [F1], on the inherited background [A1], to choose a positively oriented orthonormal coframe $(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)$ with $n^\flat=-e^0$. The definition gives $F_{0i}=-E_i/c$. For $i=1,2,3$, the component formula in [F2] gives $({\star_gF})_{10}=-F_{23}$, $({\star_gF})_{20}=-F_{31}$, and $({\star_gF})_{30}=-F_{12}$; therefore $B_1=F_{23}$, $B_2=F_{31}$, and $B_3=F_{12}$, equivalently $F_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$. The basis formula in [F2] gives $\star_g(-e^0\wedge B)=B_1e^2\wedge e^3+B_2e^3\wedge e^1+B_3e^1\wedge e^2$. Together with $n^\flat\wedge E/c=-\sum_i(E_i/c)e^0\wedge e^i$, this matches all six independent components of $F$ and proves $F=n^\flat\wedge E/c+\star_g(n^\flat\wedge B)$.

In this coframe, $F^{0i}=-F_{0i}=E_i/c$ and $F^{ij}=F_{ij}$. Antisymmetry counts each independent pair twice, so $F_{ab}F^{ab}=2\sum_{i<j}F_{ij}^2+2\sum_iF_{0i}F^{0i}=2\sum_iB_i^2-\frac{2}{c^2}\sum_iE_i^2$. The spatial coframe induces the Euclidean inner product $g^{-1}$ on the rest covectors, so these sums are $\langle B,B\rangle_n$ and $\langle E,E\rangle_n$. This proves the first invariant.

Summing over increasing $k$-tuples $I$, and writing $dx^I=dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k}$, if $\omega=\sum_I\omega_I\,dx^I$, then $$d\omega=\sum_I d\omega_I\wedge dx^I.$$
The graded vector space $$ \Omega^*(M):=\bigoplus_{k\ge 0}\Omega^k(M) $$ with the wedge product is an associative graded-commutative algebra.

**Inverse metric.** The **inverse metric** at $p$ is the symmetric bilinear form $$g_p^{-1}:T_p^*M\times T_p^*M\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta):=g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\sharp_p\beta).$$ It is symmetric because $g_p$ is, and it is nondegenerate: if $g_p^{-1}(\alpha,\beta)=0$ for all $\beta$, then $g_p(\sharp_p\alpha,\cdot)=0$, so $\sharp_p\alpha=0$ and hence $\alpha=0$.
